architectural_implications.after: A workflow skeleton of deterministic steps owns sequencing; the LLM is called only at nodes where reasoning is required, with typed input and schema-validated output.
architectural_implications.before: An autonomous agent loop decides its own next action, tool, and termination condition.
architectural_implications.consequence: Cost and token usage drop, behavior becomes reproducible and debuggable, and failures localize to a single node—at the cost of losing open-ended exploration capability.
architectural_implications.observation: Responsibility for control flow is moved out of the LLM and into deterministic code that invokes small, bounded LLM steps.

architectural_implications.after: Orchestration schedules work; execution happens in isolated, resumable microVMs; session state is addressable independently.
architectural_implications.before: A single ECS Fargate container holds both the harness and the runtime, so a run's lifespan is tied to one container.
architectural_implications.consequence: Parallel agent executions can be sandboxed and resumed, but the platform now needs explicit state serialization and lifecycle management.
architectural_implications.observation: Session state is externalized from the runtime, separating orchestration, agent runtime, and session state.

architectural_implications.after: Each agent is a single YAML file in the repository, reviewed through merge requests like any other code.
architectural_implications.before: Agent behavior is defined in prompts or UI configuration, outside normal code review and change management.
architectural_implications.consequence: Audit trails, rollback, and blast-radius review come for free from the Git workflow—but expressiveness is capped by what the YAML schema can represent.
architectural_implications.observation: The agent specification file becomes the unit of review and governance.

article_ideas.angle: Reframe agent permissions as a property of a node in a workflow graph rather than a property of the runtime, and show why that composes with code review, rollback, and audit in a way that global allowlists cannot.
article_ideas.audience: Platform and security engineers deploying LLM agents in regulated or multi-tenant environments
article_ideas.based_on: so the same harness can be read-only in one step and write-capable in another
article_ideas.thesis: Granularity of the permission boundary, not the strength of the model, determines the blast radius of an agent failure; declaring tools, network, and MCP access per step lets one harness be read-only in one node and write-capable in another, which is strictly better than either a globally-permissioned agent or a fleet of single-purpose agents each with its own deploy surface.
article_ideas.title: Least Privilege Belongs on the Workflow Node, Not the Agent

article_ideas.angle: Argue for a record-and-replay eval pyramid over agent workflow graphs, and specify what must be captured per node to make replay faithful (state, context, tool observations, not just the prompt).
article_ideas.audience: AI engineers and QA leads running internal automation platforms
article_ideas.based_on: Instead of constructing synthetic end-to-end scenarios
article_ideas.thesis: Teams building agent workflows default to synthetic end-to-end scenarios because that is the only test shape they know, then abandon evals as too expensive and too noisy; capturing per-step inputs from real production runs and replaying them turns each node into a regression unit test, and the residual risk of missed cross-step interactions is a measurable quantity rather than an article of faith.
article_ideas.title: Your Agent Evals Are Integration Tests When They Should Be Unit Tests

article_ideas.angle: Frame the architecture as an adopted, untrusted reasoning core surrounded by an owned control plane, and enumerate what must be built on the outside to make that posture defensible.
article_ideas.audience: Engineering leaders making platform build/buy decisions for internal agent infrastructure
article_ideas.based_on: Focuses engineering effort on workflow definition rather than building custom harnesses
article_ideas.thesis: The build-versus-adopt question for an agent harness is usually answered wrong: teams reimplement a reasoning loop they cannot maintain and then have no budget left for the control layers that actually determine whether the system is safe. Reusing a mature harness and constraining it externally with per-step permissions, strict schemas, and step boundaries moves engineering effort to the only part that is genuinely yours.
article_ideas.title: Adopt the Loop, Own the Control Plane

article_ideas.angle: Position agent specification files as infrastructure-as-code and derive the concrete review practices (blast-radius review, permission diffs, rollback) that follow for free.
article_ideas.audience: Engineers and compliance-adjacent reviewers who must change-control AI behavior
article_ideas.based_on: Agent definitions are promoted to repository artifacts
article_ideas.thesis: Declarative agent specs are worth their constraints because they co-opt Git as the audit, review, and rollback mechanism for AI behavior; the win is not readability but the fact that a behavior change becomes a diffable merge request, and the cost is a hard expressivity ceiling that teams should plan for instead of discovering mid-migration.
article_ideas.title: YAML Is a Governance Surface, Not a Config Format

connections.relationship: Applies classical least-privilege to LLM tool grants, with the workflow node rather than the service as the privilege boundary.
Schema validation is the bridge that lets probabilistic model output be consumed by deterministic branching logic.
Agent behavior inherits review, diffing, rollback, and audit properties already established for IaC.
Turns captured production state into a regression corpus, analogous to record-and-replay testing for distributed systems.
Externalized state is the prerequisite for resumable microVM execution and independent scaling of orchestration.

evidence_quotes.text: Restricts network access, available tools, skills, and MCP servers per step in the YAML file.
Code review step can read and search code but cannot edit files or push changes.

core_insights.generalization: Treat tool/network permissions as a per-node property of the workflow graph rather than a global config of the agent runtime; this composes with any harness that supports tool allowlists.
core_insights.insight: Agent capability should be bounded per workflow step, not per agent: each LLM step declares its own allowed network access, tools, skills, and MCP servers in the YAML definition, so the same harness can be read-only in one step and write-capable in another.
core_insights.why_it_matters: Least-privilege at step granularity shrinks the blast radius of a single bad model decision without requiring a separate agent per permission set, and makes permission review a plain code-review activity.

evidence_quotes.text: Evaluating individual LLM steps using historical state is cheaper and more reproducible than end-to-end synthetic benchmarks.
Injecting exact historical state and context directly into workflow nodes.

core_insights.generalization: Persist per-node inputs from real runs as a replay corpus; evaluations then become unit tests over a workflow graph rather than integration tests over a stochastic whole.
core_insights.insight: The reliability unit is the LLM step, not the end-to-end agent: individual steps are evaluated by injecting the exact historical state and context captured from production into that node, instead of constructing synthetic end-to-end scenarios.
core_insights.why_it_matters: Historical-state replay makes prompt changes and model swaps cheaply testable and regression-detectable, addressing the cost and noisiness that make synthetic end-to-end benchmarks impractical for internal automation.

evidence_quotes.text: Strict JSON schemas ensure downstream execution branches are driven by deterministic control flow.
Schema validation triggering automatic retry or fallback paths.

core_insights.generalization: Any place where you would branch on model output should be a schema-validated boundary; treat schema violations as a first-class failure mode with a defined recovery path.
core_insights.insight: Strict JSON schemas convert an unreliable free-text model call into a typed contract, so downstream branching, retries, and fallbacks are handled by deterministic control flow rather than by the model.
core_insights.why_it_matters: Validation failure becomes an explicit, observable error path (retry or fallback) instead of silent semantic drift propagating through the pipeline, which is what makes deterministic orchestration around LLM steps actually safe.

evidence_quotes.text: Every agent in Orbit is defined by a single YAML file in the repository that goes through merge request reviews just like any other code.
YAML is familiar to engineers and keeps the codebase AI-friendly.

core_insights.generalization: Prefer declarative, diffable agent specifications over UI-configured or prompt-string-defined agents wherever reviewability and audit history are requirements.
core_insights.insight: Agent definitions are promoted to repository artifacts: one YAML file per agent, merged and reviewed through the same merge-request process as application code.
core_insights.why_it_matters: It co-opts existing Git governance, review, and audit trails for agent behavior, which is the cheapest way to make AI behavior change-controlled in a regulated environment, and it raises readability for engineers who must debug or amend workflows.

evidence_quotes.text: Evolution from a single ECS Fargate container containing harness and runtime to separated layers: Orchestration, Agent Runtime, and Session State, leveraging AWS Lambda microVMs.
Fargate limits like lack of package managers are solved using AWS Lambda microVMs for resumable, isolated execution.

core_insights.generalization: Design agent platforms so that execution is ephemeral and state is externalized; then isolation, resumability, and concurrency control become separate, independently tunable concerns.
core_insights.insight: The agent runtime was decomposed from a single container hosting both harness and runtime into three separated layers (orchestration, agent runtime, session state), with session state made resumable on AWS Lambda microVMs because the container platform lacked package managers.
core_insights.why_it_matters: Separating session state from execution is what enables resumption and isolated sandboxing per run, and it means orchestration can scale independently of the compute that hosts agent sessions.

evidence_quotes.text: Flywire reuses the harness behind Claude Code (Claude Agent SDK) out-of-the-box and adds control layers on top.
Focuses engineering effort on workflow definition rather than building custom harnesses.

core_insights.generalization: Constrain an adopted agent loop from the outside (permissions, schemas, step boundaries) rather than reimplementing the loop; reserve custom harness work for cases where the control surface is genuinely absent.
core_insights.insight: Reusing a mature agent harness (the Claude Agent SDK, the harness behind Claude Code) out-of-the-box shifts engineering effort from harness construction to workflow definition and control layers.
core_insights.why_it_matters: The build-versus-adopt decision for the harness is where most agent teams burn time; adopting a proven loop and constraining it externally is a materially cheaper path to production than writing a bespoke reasoning loop.

evidence_quotes.text: Timeouts, rate limits, and concurrency locks to prevent runaway agent spawning.

core_insights.generalization: Any system where an agent can request more agents/compute needs explicit admission control at the orchestrator; treat fan-out as a capacity-planning problem, not a model-behavior problem.
core_insights.insight: Runaway agent spawning is treated as an operational failure mode addressed with floor-level controls—timeouts, rate limits, and concurrency locks—rather than with better prompting.
core_insights.why_it_matters: Concurrency control is the difference between a bounded cost envelope and an unbounded one when thousands of workflow executions can fan out; these controls belong in the orchestration layer, not in the agent's reasoning.

evidence_quotes.text: Restricts network access, available tools, skills, and MCP servers per step in the YAML file.
Code review step can read and search code but cannot edit files or push changes.

deep_dives.research_question: When a workflow node is granted a read-only tool set, at which layer (harness allowlist, sandbox syscall/filesystem boundary, or orchestrator) must the restriction be enforced so that tool chaining, MCP servers, or prompt injection cannot escalate to file writes or network egress?
deep_dives.topic: Enforcement layer for per-step capability grants
deep_dives.trigger_insight: Agent capability should be bounded per workflow step, not per agent
deep_dives.why: Per-step least privilege is only worth the YAML complexity if the restriction is adversarially sound; if the boundary lives in the prompt or the harness's cooperative tool filter, a compliant-looking workflow file is a false sense of security in a PCI/SOC-scoped environment.

evidence_quotes.text: Evaluating individual LLM steps using historical state is cheaper and more reproducible than end-to-end synthetic benchmarks.
Injecting exact historical state and context directly into workflow nodes.

deep_dives.research_question: Do regressions detected by replaying historical state into individual LLM steps predict actual end-to-end workflow failures in production, and what is the false-negative rate of a step-only eval suite relative to end-to-end scenario testing?
deep_dives.topic: Correlation between step-level replay evals and end-to-end workflow outcomes
deep_dives.trigger_insight: The reliability unit is the LLM step, not the end-to-end agent
deep_dives.why: The whole economic argument for step-level evaluation rests on an unmeasured assumption of agreement; if step replay systematically misses cross-step interaction failures, teams will ship regressions that their tests declare green.

evidence_quotes.text: Strict JSON schemas ensure downstream execution branches are driven by deterministic control flow.
Schema validation triggering automatic retry or fallback paths.

deep_dives.research_question: What is the observed schema-validation failure rate per LLM step in production, and how should the retry/fallback split be budgeted so that a failing step degrades deterministically instead of converting into retry storms or silent semantic drift?
deep_dives.topic: Schema violations as a first-class failure mode with a recovery budget
deep_dives.trigger_insight: Strict JSON schemas convert an unreliable free-text model call into a typed contract
deep_dives.why: Schemas are described as the bridge that makes probabilistic output safe to branch on, but the operational cost of that bridge (retry latency, token spend, fallback quality) determines whether the boundary is a control or just a tax.

evidence_quotes.text: Every agent in Orbit is defined by a single YAML file in the repository that goes through merge request reviews just like any other code.
YAML is familiar to engineers and keeps the codebase AI-friendly.

deep_dives.research_question: At what workflow complexity (loop depth, dynamic fan-out, conditional branching over structured state) do authors of YAML-defined agents start needing escape hatches into general-purpose code, and how much reviewability is lost when they do?
deep_dives.topic: Expressivity ceiling of a single-file declarative agent spec
deep_dives.trigger_insight: What is the expressivity ceiling of a single-YAML-file agent definition before workflows need real programming-language constructs
deep_dives.why: The governance benefit of YAML-reviewed agents is bounded by the schema's expressiveness; knowing where that ceiling sits tells teams when to split a workflow versus when to reach for code, and prevents the schema from becoming a leaky abstraction with hidden scripts.

open_questions.question: How are per-step tool and network restrictions actually enforced—at the harness, the sandbox, or the orchestration layer—and can a model step circumvent them?

project_ideas.based_on: Restricts network access, available tools, skills, and MCP servers per step in the YAML file.
project_ideas.hypothesis: A workflow node granted only read tools can be driven to perform a file write or outbound network call via tool chaining, MCP server invocation, or injected instructions when the restriction is enforced at the harness allowlist layer, but cannot when the same grant is enforced at the sandbox boundary — so the escape rate is a function of enforcement layer, not of the permission declaration.
project_ideas.measurement: Successful escapes per 100 attempts per enforcement layer, broken down by attack vector; a nonzero harness-only rate with a zero sandbox rate confirms the hypothesis, while any sandbox escape falsifies it.
project_ideas.name: StepBoundary
project_ideas.poc: Build a minimal 3-step YAML workflow (read-only code search node, reasoning node, write node) running on a containerized agent harness, implement the per-step restriction twice — harness tool-allowlist only, and harness allowlist plus a syscall/egress-denying microVM sandbox — and run a fixed red-team suite of escalation attempts (MCP shim, prompt injection in retrieved file content, tool-argument confusion) against both configurations.

project_ideas.based_on: Evaluating individual LLM steps using historical state is cheaper and more reproducible than end-to-end synthetic benchmarks.
project_ideas.hypothesis: Step-level replay evaluations rank a set of candidate prompt/model changes in the same order as end-to-end workflow evaluations with high agreement, but under-report failures whose cause is inter-step interaction — giving a measurable false-negative rate rather than an assumed one.
project_ideas.measurement: Spearman rank correlation between step-level and end-to-end pass rates across the 20 changes, plus the count of changes that pass all step replays but fail end-to-end; report the false-negative rate and per-evaluation cost delta.
project_ideas.name: Replay Agreement Study
project_ideas.poc: Instrument a 4-5 step internal workflow to persist per-node inputs and outputs from production, build a replay harness that injects historical state into single nodes, then take 20 candidate changes (prompt edits, model swaps) and evaluate each both by step-level replay and by end-to-end runs on a held-out set of real trigger events.

project_ideas.based_on: Schema validation triggering automatic retry or fallback paths.
project_ideas.hypothesis: Schema-validation failures cluster in a small number of steps and failure classes, so a per-step recovery policy tuned to the observed failure taxonomy (bounded retry for malformed output, fallback for semantic mismatch) reduces failed workflow runs more than a uniform retry-everything policy at lower token cost.
project_ideas.measurement: Validation failure rate per step, recovery success rate and additional tokens consumed per failure class, and end-to-end workflow completion rate under each policy; the hypothesis holds if class-specific recovery improves completion rate at lower mean token cost per successful run.
project_ideas.name: Schema Recovery Budget
project_ideas.poc: Instrument a schema-validated workflow to log every validation failure with the offending payload and the resolved recovery path, classify failures into malformed-JSON, missing-field, enum-mismatch, and semantically-wrong-but-valid, then A/B a uniform 3x retry policy against a class-specific retry/fallback policy.

summary.html:
Overview

  • Speaker: Eduardo Simon & Javier Casal
  • Channel: AI Engineer
  • Main topic: Building practical, structured, and compliant AI agent workflows in-house at Flywire
  • Purpose: To share Flywire's engineering journey and technical architecture for building practical, compliant, and reliable AI agent workflows rather than open-ended LLM loops. Eduardo Simon and Javier Casal from Flywire discuss their AI platform 'Orbit', which transitions AI agents from open-ended autonomous 'autopilot' loops into structured, workflow-driven tools. Operating in the heavily regulated global payments space (PCI DSS, SOC II), Flywire requires strict security, data privacy, and deterministic control. Orbit uses YAML-defined workflows, reuses the Claude Agent SDK with strict network, tool, and skill restrictions, and implements isolated evaluations and YAML-first developer tooling.

Topic Map

Context and Compliance at Flywire

  • Explanation: Introduction to Flywire's scale (5300+ clients, 240+ countries) and the absolute necessity of strict compliance frameworks like PCI DSS and SOC II when handling high-value global payments.
  • Key claims:
    • Regulatory compliance, privacy, and security are core requirements, not optional.
    • Customer data, PII, and payment details must remain completely safe.
  • Examples:
    • Processing transactions across education, healthcare, travel, and B2B.
  • Terminology:
    • PCI DSS
    • SOC II
    • PII
    • PHI
  • Why it matters: Financial enterprises cannot pass sensitive payment data to ungoverned third-party endpoints without strict architectural boundaries.

Orbit: The Toil Killer

  • Explanation: Orbit is Flywire's internal platform that eliminates daily engineering repetitive tasks by combining deterministic code with structured LLM workflow steps.
  • Key claims:
    • Instead of open-ended LLM loops, Orbit pairs deterministic code with small LLM steps.
    • Repetitive procedural logic is written in code, and LLMs are called only where reasoning is needed.
  • Examples:
    • Code review agents, linter fixes, translation workflows, and support ticket triage.
  • Terminology:
    • Orbit
    • toil killer
    • workflow-oriented
  • Why it matters: Reduces AI token usage, costs, and unpredictability while ensuring enterprise-grade reliability.

Anatomy of a Workflow & YAML-First Authoring

  • Explanation: Every agent in Orbit is defined by a single YAML file in the repository that goes through merge request reviews just like any other code.
  • Key claims:
    • Workflows start with a trigger (webhook, API, schedule), execute deterministic steps, and use strict LLM steps with bounded permissions.
    • YAML is familiar to engineers and keeps the codebase AI-friendly.
  • Examples:
    • Code review agent triggered by a GitLab webhook.
  • Terminology:
    • YAML
    • merge request review
    • trigger
    • deterministic steps
  • Why it matters: Enables engineers to read, write, and review agent workflow definitions as easily as regular application code.

Technical Architecture: Victoria, Fargate, and MicroVMs

  • Explanation: Evolution from a single ECS Fargate container containing harness and runtime to separated layers: Orchestration, Agent Runtime, and Session State, leveraging AWS Lambda microVMs.
  • Key claims:
    • Separating orchestration, runtime, and session state improves isolation, maintainability, and resource allocation.
    • Fargate limits like lack of package managers are solved using AWS Lambda microVMs for resumable, isolated execution.
  • Examples:
    • Timeouts, rate limits, and concurrency locks to prevent runaway agent spawning.
  • Terminology:
    • Victoria
    • ECS Fargate
    • AWS Lambda MicroVMs
    • Orchestration layer
  • Why it matters: Ensures scalability, cost control, and sandboxing across thousands of parallel agent executions.

Reusing the Claude Agent SDK with Limits

  • Explanation: Flywire reuses the harness behind Claude Code (Claude Agent SDK) out-of-the-box and adds control layers on top.
  • Key claims:
    • Restricts network access, available tools, skills, and MCP servers per step in the YAML file.
    • Focuses engineering effort on workflow definition rather than building custom harnesses.
  • Examples:
    • Code review step can read and search code but cannot edit files or push changes.
  • Terminology:
    • Claude Agent SDK
    • MCP servers
    • harness
  • Why it matters: Leverages mature, well-tested agent harnesses while maintaining strict enterprise security controls.

Evaluations: Structured Outputs and Isolated Evals

  • Explanation: Reliability is achieved through strict JSON schemas for model responses and isolated component evaluation using historical state.
  • Key claims:
    • Strict JSON schemas ensure downstream execution branches are driven by deterministic control flow.
    • Evaluating individual LLM steps using historical state is cheaper and more reproducible than end-to-end synthetic benchmarks.
  • Examples:
    • Schema validation triggering automatic retry or fallback paths.
  • Terminology:
    • Structured outputs
    • JSON schema
    • isolated evaluation
    • golden dataset
  • Why it matters: Solves the noisiness and high cost of traditional synthetic end-to-end benchmark evaluations.

Key Points

Workflows, Not Autopilot

  • Explanation: AI agents should operate within structured, deterministic workflows rather than free-roaming open-ended loops.
  • Evidence: Orbit pairs deterministic code with small LLM steps, calling models only when reasoning is needed.
  • Practical implication: Improves control, safety, and reliability while reducing costs.

YAML-First Developer Experience

  • Explanation: Defining agents in YAML files allows engineers to use existing Git workflows and merge request reviews.
  • Evidence: Every agent in Orbit is a single YAML file reviewed like any other code.
  • Practical implication: Lowers adoption barrier for engineering teams and keeps codebase AI-friendly.

Isolated Component Evaluation

  • Explanation: Testing individual LLM workflow steps with historical state rather than full end-to-end runs.
  • Evidence: Injecting exact historical state and context directly into workflow nodes.
  • Practical implication: Makes evaluating model output quality, prompt adjustments, and regression catching cheaper and faster.

Frameworks, Models & Processes

Orbit Workflow Framework

  • How it works: Combines deterministic code triggers, structured activities, and constrained LLM steps defined in YAML.
  • Components:
    • Trigger (API, Webhook, Schedule, MCP server)
    • Deterministic steps (metadata fetching, risk tiering, cloning)
    • LLM step (read-only tools, strict JSON schema output)
    • Deterministic output handler (posting back findings)
  • When to use: Automating repetitive internal engineering tasks like code reviews, dependency updates, and ticket triage.

Examples & Case Studies

Building the Victoria Linter Fixer agent

  • Illustrates: Automated code review and refactoring across hundreds of repositories
  • Lesson: Automating linter findings fixes saves thousands of manual engineering hours.

Actionable Takeaways

  • Immediate:
    • Start small with high-impact, repetitive tasks like code review or linter fixes.
    • Enforce strict JSON schemas on all LLM outputs to guarantee deterministic downstream control flow.
    • Use YAML for workflow definitions to integrate smoothly with existing CI/CD and MR processes.
  • Strategic:
    • Build internal platforms (like Orbit) to keep sensitive data within your secure environment.
    • Separate orchestration, runtime, and session state to scale agent infrastructure independently.
    • Move from vibe checks to versioned golden datasets extracted from real OpenTelemetry execution traces.
  • Questions to investigate:
    • How can full container sandboxing (Docker-in-Docker) be achieved securely at scale?
    • How to implement automated model routers for cost-aware multi-vendor model selection?

Claims Worth Verifying

  • Over 9,000 code review agent runs completed in the last 30 days averaging under 3 minutes per merge request. (Metric / Operational Impact)
  • Over 11,000 total workflow runs across Flywire engineering with a 99% success rate. (Metric / Operational Impact)

Notable Quotes

"Agents in Orbit: Workflows, Not Autopilot" (at 0:00) "Orbit is an internal platform that eliminates daily engineering repetitive tasks by including LLMs directly into structured workflows." (at 5:05)

Compressed Summary

  • Orbit combines deterministic code with structured LLM workflow steps.
  • Agents are defined in YAML and reviewed via standard merge requests.
  • Strict JSON schemas and isolated step evaluations guarantee reliability.
  • Reusing Claude Agent SDK with strict tool and network bounds ensures security.
  • Keywords: agents, workflows, yaml, compliance, evaluations
  • Core insight: Structured, workflow-driven automation transforms AI agents into reliable, secure force multipliers for enterprise engineering teams.

  - Regulatory compliance, privacy, and security are core requirements, not optional.
  - Customer data, PII, and payment details must remain completely safe.
- **Examples**:
  - Processing transactions across education, healthcare, travel, and B2B.
- **Terminology**:
  - PCI DSS
  - SOC II
  - PII
  - PHI
- **Why it matters**: Financial enterprises cannot pass sensitive payment data to ungoverned third-party endpoints without strict architectural boundaries.
### Orbit: The Toil Killer
- **Explanation**: Orbit is Flywire's internal platform that eliminates daily engineering repetitive tasks by combining deterministic code with structured LLM workflow steps.
- **Key claims**:
  - Instead of open-ended LLM loops, Orbit pairs deterministic code with small LLM steps.
  - Repetitive procedural logic is written in code, and LLMs are called only where reasoning is needed.
- **Examples**:
  - Code review agents, linter fixes, translation workflows, and support ticket triage.
- **Terminology**:
  - Orbit
  - toil killer
  - workflow-oriented
- **Why it matters**: Reduces AI token usage, costs, and unpredictability while ensuring enterprise-grade reliability.
### Anatomy of a Workflow & YAML-First Authoring
- **Explanation**: Every agent in Orbit is defined by a single YAML file in the repository that goes through merge request reviews just like any other code.
- **Key claims**:
  - Workflows start with a trigger (webhook, API, schedule), execute deterministic steps, and use strict LLM steps with bounded permissions.
  - YAML is familiar to engineers and keeps the codebase AI-friendly.
- **Examples**:
  - Code review agent triggered by a GitLab webhook.
- **Terminology**:
  - YAML
  - merge request review
  - trigger
  - deterministic steps
- **Why it matters**: Enables engineers to read, write, and review agent workflow definitions as easily as regular application code.
### Technical Architecture: Victoria, Fargate, and MicroVMs
- **Explanation**: Evolution from a single ECS Fargate container containing harness and runtime to separated layers: Orchestration, Agent Runtime, and Session State, leveraging AWS Lambda microVMs.
- **Key claims**:
  - Separating orchestration, runtime, and session state improves isolation, maintainability, and resource allocation.
  - Fargate limits like lack of package managers are solved using AWS Lambda microVMs for resumable, isolated execution.
- **Examples**:
  - Timeouts, rate limits, and concurrency locks to prevent runaway agent spawning.
- **Terminology**:
  - Victoria
  - ECS Fargate
  - AWS Lambda MicroVMs
  - Orchestration layer
- **Why it matters**: Ensures scalability, cost control, and sandboxing across thousands of parallel agent executions.
### Reusing the Claude Agent SDK with Limits
- **Explanation**: Flywire reuses the harness behind Claude Code (Claude Agent SDK) out-of-the-box and adds control layers on top.
- **Key claims**:
  - Restricts network access, available tools, skills, and MCP servers per step in the YAML file.
  - Focuses engineering effort on workflow definition rather than building custom harnesses.
- **Examples**:
  - Code review step can read and search code but cannot edit files or push changes.
- **Terminology**:
  - Claude Agent SDK
  - MCP servers
  - harness
- **Why it matters**: Leverages mature, well-tested agent harnesses while maintaining strict enterprise security controls.
### Evaluations: Structured Outputs and Isolated Evals
- **Explanation**: Reliability is achieved through strict JSON schemas for model responses and isolated component evaluation using historical state.
- **Key claims**:
  - Strict JSON schemas ensure downstream execution branches are driven by deterministic control flow.
  - Evaluating individual LLM steps using historical state is cheaper and more reproducible than end-to-end synthetic benchmarks.
- **Examples**:
  - Schema validation triggering automatic retry or fallback paths.
- **Terminology**:
  - Structured outputs
  - JSON schema
  - isolated evaluation
  - golden dataset
- **Why it matters**: Solves the noisiness and high cost of traditional synthetic end-to-end benchmark evaluations.
## Key Points
### Workflows, Not Autopilot
- **Explanation**: AI agents should operate within structured, deterministic workflows rather than free-roaming open-ended loops.
- **Evidence**: Orbit pairs deterministic code with small LLM steps, calling models only when reasoning is needed.
- **Practical implication**: Improves control, safety, and reliability while reducing costs.
### YAML-First Developer Experience
- **Explanation**: Defining agents in YAML files allows engineers to use existing Git workflows and merge request reviews.
- **Evidence**: Every agent in Orbit is a single YAML file reviewed like any other code.
- **Practical implication**: Lowers adoption barrier for engineering teams and keeps codebase AI-friendly.
### Isolated Component Evaluation
- **Explanation**: Testing individual LLM workflow steps with historical state rather than full end-to-end runs.
- **Evidence**: Injecting exact historical state and context directly into workflow nodes.
- **Practical implication**: Makes evaluating model output quality, prompt adjustments, and regression catching cheaper and faster.
## Frameworks, Models & Processes
### Orbit Workflow Framework
- **How it works**: Combines deterministic code triggers, structured activities, and constrained LLM steps defined in YAML.
- **Components**:
  - Trigger (API, Webhook, Schedule, MCP server)
  - Deterministic steps (metadata fetching, risk tiering, cloning)
  - LLM step (read-only tools, strict JSON schema output)
  - Deterministic output handler (posting back findings)
- **When to use**: Automating repetitive internal engineering tasks like code reviews, dependency updates, and ticket triage.
## Examples & Case Studies
### Building the Victoria Linter Fixer agent
- **Illustrates**: Automated code review and refactoring across hundreds of repositories
- **Lesson**: Automating linter findings fixes saves thousands of manual engineering hours.
## Actionable Takeaways
- **Immediate**:
  - Start small with high-impact, repetitive tasks like code review or linter fixes.
  - Enforce strict JSON schemas on all LLM outputs to guarantee deterministic downstream control flow.
  - Use YAML for workflow definitions to integrate smoothly with existing CI/CD and MR processes.
- **Strategic**:
  - Build internal platforms (like Orbit) to keep sensitive data within your secure environment.
  - Separate orchestration, runtime, and session state to scale agent infrastructure independently.
  - Move from vibe checks to versioned golden datasets extracted from real OpenTelemetry execution traces.
- **Questions to investigate**:
  - How can full container sandboxing (Docker-in-Docker) be achieved securely at scale?
  - How to implement automated model routers for cost-aware multi-vendor model selection?
## Claims Worth Verifying
- Over 9,000 code review agent runs completed in the last 30 days averaging under 3 minutes per merge request. (Metric / Operational Impact)
- Over 11,000 total workflow runs across Flywire engineering with a 99% success rate. (Metric / Operational Impact)

> "Agents in Orbit: Workflows, Not Autopilot" (at 0:00)
> "Orbit is an internal platform that eliminates daily engineering repetitive tasks by including LLMs directly into structured workflows." (at 5:05)
## Compressed Summary
- Orbit combines deterministic code with structured LLM workflow steps.
- Agents are defined in YAML and reviewed via standard merge requests.
- Strict JSON schemas and isolated step evaluations guarantee reliability.
- Reusing Claude Agent SDK with strict tool and network bounds ensures security.
- **Keywords**: agents, workflows, yaml, compliance, evaluations
- **Core insight**: Structured, workflow-driven automation transforms AI agents into reliable, secure force multipliers for enterprise engineering teams.
